questions.q: A like counter shows slightly different values on different devices for a few seconds before settling on the same number everywhere. What does this illustrate?
options: A bug that must be fixed with strong consistency immediately
Eventual consistency, chosen deliberately because speed and availability matter more than instant synchronization for this data
A violation of the CAP theorem
A failure of the message queue delivering the like event
questions.explain: Brief, temporary disagreement between replicas that converges over time is the definition of eventual consistency — a deliberate trade-off, not a defect, for low-stakes data like a like count.

questions.q: A payment service calls a slow, intermittently timing-out shipping API, and soon the payment service itself becomes unresponsive to its own callers. What combination of patterns would have prevented this?
options: Increasing the number of database replicas
A circuit breaker (to stop calling the failing dependency) and a bulkhead (to isolate its resource pool from the rest of the system)
Switching from asynchronous to synchronous communication
Removing all timeouts from the system
questions.explain: This is a cascading failure caused by resource exhaustion. A circuit breaker stops the pileup of waiting calls, and a bulkhead isolates the failing dependency's resource pool so unrelated requests aren't affected.

questions.q: Three nodes lose contact with the rest of a cluster for 30 seconds. If the system wants both sides to keep accepting writes to the same data during that window, what trade-off and follow-up mechanism does it need?
options: A CP choice, with no further mechanism needed
An AP choice, plus a conflict-resolution strategy like last-write-wins or a CRDT to reconcile the two sides once the partition heals
No trade-off is needed; CAP does not apply to small clusters
A rate limiter to prevent writes during the partition
questions.explain: Allowing writes on both sides of a partition favors availability over consistency (an AP choice), and reconciling the resulting divergence afterward requires an explicit conflict-resolution mechanism.

questions.q: Which lesson's concept explains why a checkout system can treat inventory count and payment state with two different consistency models in the same system?
options: Observability — different metrics require different dashboards
The CAP theorem — different pieces of data can reasonably make different consistency-vs-availability trade-offs based on what they're used for
Idempotency — different operations need different retry keys
Backpressure — different queues need different capacities
questions.explain: The CAP theorem's consistency-vs-availability trade-off is applied per piece of data, not uniformly across a whole system — the case study showed inventory favoring availability and payment favoring consistency.

questions.q: Across the whole course, what is the common thread connecting asynchronous communication, heartbeats/timeouts, and idempotent retries?
options: They are all unrelated, independently invented techniques
They all exist because a distributed system can never be fully certain whether a remote node or message succeeded, only infer it — so systems are built to act safely under that uncertainty
They are all specific only to Salesforce's Apex runtime
They all eliminate the need for a network entirely
questions.explain: The course's throughline is that distributed systems can only infer, never confirm, the state of a remote node or message — asynchronous design, failure detection by timeout, and idempotent retries are all ways of acting safely despite that unavoidable uncertainty.
